threats.description: An env variable, header or URL query parameter of this MCP server holds a literal credential instead of a reference such as ${API_KEY}, ${env:API_KEY} or ${input:api-key}. MCP config files such as .mcp.json and .vscode/mcp.json are meant to be committed and shared, so the credential ends up in version control and on every machine that clones the repository.
threats.mitigation: Remove the value from the file and rotate the credential. Reference it from the environment instead (${VAR} in Claude Code, ${env:VAR} in Cursor and Windsurf) or use a VS Code input variable (${input:id}) so the client prompts for it and stores it securely.
threats.title: Literal credential in MCP server configuration

threats.description: The server starts through npx, bunx, pnpm dlx, yarn dlx, uvx, docker or podman with a package or image that has no fixed version (no @version, ==version, image tag or digest, or a floating tag such as latest). Every launch can fetch new code, so a compromised release, a typosquatted or hallucinated package name, or a hijacked maintainer account runs on the developer's machine with access to whatever the agent can reach.
threats.mitigation: Pin an exact version (npx -y package@1.2.3, uvx package==1.2.3) or an image digest (image@sha256:...), and review changes before raising it.
threats.title: MCP server launched from an unpinned package or image

threats.description: A filesystem server is given /, a home directory or a whole Windows drive as an allowed root. The agent can then read and change SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser profiles and every other project on the machine, and a prompt injection in any document it reads inherits that reach.
threats.mitigation: Pass only the project directories the agent needs as allowed roots, and keep credential directories such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws out of them.
threats.title: Filesystem MCP server rooted at the whole disk or home directory

threats.description: The configured server exists to run shell or terminal commands for the agent, either a package known for this (such as @wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander, mcp-server-commands or mcp-shell-server) or an MCP package whose name marks it as a shell or terminal server. Any prompt injection that reaches the agent can then run arbitrary commands with the user's privileges.
threats.mitigation: Remove the server where a narrower tool would do. Otherwise run it in a container or sandbox without credentials, restrict it to an allowlist of commands, and require human approval for every call.
threats.title: MCP server gives the agent shell command execution

threats.description: The server starts through npx, bunx, pnpm dlx, yarn dlx, uvx, docker or podman with a package or image that has no fixed version (no @version, ==version, image tag or digest, or a floating tag such as latest). Every launch can fetch new code, so a compromised release, a typosquatted or hallucinated package name, or a hijacked maintainer account runs on the developer's machine with access to whatever the agent can reach.
threats.mitigation: Pin an exact version (npx -y package@1.2.3, uvx package==1.2.3) or an image digest (image@sha256:...), and review changes before raising it.
threats.title: MCP server launched from an unpinned package or image

threats.description: The server runs through docker run or podman run with --privileged, host networking or another host namespace, a dangerous added capability, an unconfined seccomp or AppArmor profile, or a bind mount of / or the container runtime socket. Each of these lets code in the container reach the host, which defeats the reason for containerizing the server.
threats.mitigation: Drop --privileged and host namespaces, mount only the directories the server needs (read-only where possible), never mount the Docker socket, and add --cap-drop=ALL with only the capabilities the server requires.
threats.title: Containerized MCP server launched with host-level privileges

threats.description: The server URL uses http:// or ws:// to a host that is not loopback. Tool calls, tool results and any credentials sent in headers cross the network in cleartext, where anyone on the path can read or modify them.
threats.mitigation: Use an https:// (or wss://) URL. Reserve plain http for servers bound to localhost.
threats.title: Remote MCP server over unencrypted HTTP

threats.description: The config points at a remote MCP server but sets no Authorization or API key header, no OAuth settings and no header helper. Clients that follow the MCP authorization spec discover OAuth at connect time, so the server may still require sign-in; the config alone cannot show that. If the server accepts anonymous calls, anyone who learns the URL can use its tools and data.
threats.mitigation: Confirm the server requires authentication. Prefer servers that implement MCP OAuth authorization, or pass a credential through a header that references an environment or input variable.
threats.title: Remote MCP server with no credentials configured
